subject: physics
title: The Solar System
key_idea: The Solar System is the Sun, eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets. The Sun formed from a cloud of dust and gas pulled together by gravity. Our model of the Solar System has changed as telescopes and space missions gave new evidence.

sections.heading: What is in the Solar System

blocks.text: (Physics only, not needed for Combined Science) The Solar System is the Sun and everything that orbits it. It is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy.

All planets orbit the Sun, each in its own orbit.

items: The Solar System has one star, eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets.
Planets, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets orbit the Sun. Moons orbit planets.
The planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

blocks.text: The Sun formed from a cloud of dust and gas called a nebula.

items.text: Gravity pulls the dust and gas together.
Gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy, so the core becomes very hot and dense.
The temperature and pressure become high enough for nuclear fusion to begin.
The inward pull of gravity is balanced by the outward push from the energy released in fusion, so the star is stable.

blocks.text: Fusion happens in the Sun because of the high temperature, the high pressure and the large gravitational forces from its large mass.

items: The Sun formed from a nebula pulled together by gravity.
Fusion starts when the core is hot and dense enough.
A stable star has gravity balanced by the energy from fusion.

sections.heading: How ideas about the Solar System have changed

blocks.text: Observations have changed our model of the Solar System over time.

items: Long ago the Earth was believed to be at the centre, with the planets, the Moon and the Sun orbiting it.
In 1543 Copernicus proposed that the Earth is a planet, and that the Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun.
Telescope observations supported the **Sun-centred model**. Galileo saw moons orbiting Jupiter, so not everything orbits the Earth.
Later telescopes discovered the planets Uranus and Neptune and the asteroid belt.
Photographs, computer modelling, satellites and space probes such as Voyager gave more evidence.
The Earth-centred model was replaced by a Sun-centred model.
Telescope evidence, such as the moons of Jupiter, supported the change.
New technology keeps adding to the evidence.

checks.q: Give three types of object, other than the Sun, that form the Solar System.
checks.a: Any three from: planets, dwarf planets, moons (natural satellites), asteroids, comets.

checks.q: Describe how the Sun was formed.
checks.a: A cloud of dust and gas (nebula) was drawn together by gravity. Gravitational potential energy was transferred to kinetic energy, so the core became very hot and dense. A protostar formed and nuclear fusion began.

checks.q: Explain how observing the moons of Jupiter supported a Sun-centred Solar System.
checks.a: The moons were seen orbiting Jupiter. This showed that not everything orbits the Earth.

worked_example.question:
The Universe contains many stars. The Sun is the star at the centre of our Solar System.

Give three other types of object that form our Solar System.
answer_points: Asteroids, meteors, meteoroids, meteorites or comets are also allowed.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each type of object.

worked_example.question:
More than two thousand years ago the Earth was believed to be at the centre of the universe.
The planets, the Moon and the Sun were believed to be in orbit around the Earth.
In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus proposed that the Earth was a planet, and that the Earth and the other planets orbit around the Sun.

Discuss how evidence has changed our views of the universe.
answer_points: Telescope evidence supported the Sun-centred model.
Galileo observed the moons of Jupiter. They rotate around Jupiter, so not everything rotates about the Earth.
Other telescope observations include the discovery of Uranus, Neptune and the asteroid belt.
Detailed photographic evidence, computer modelling and satellite observations added to the evidence.
Space probes such as the Voyager missions verified the Sun-centred model.
worked_example.tip: A six-mark level-marked answer. Higher levels need accurate, detailed and logically structured physics throughout.

blocks.text: This course also covers minor planets, and geostationary and polar orbits for artificial satellites. A polar orbit travels over both poles.
Moons are natural satellites. Artificial satellites are made by people and launched into orbit.

The Sun is a star.

Describe how the Sun was formed.
answer_points: It formed from a cloud of dust and gas (a nebula).
The dust and gas were drawn together by gravitational force.
Gravitational potential energy was transferred to kinetic energy.
The core became very hot and dense and a protostar formed.
